samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both forms are close. Each uses visible labels, selects for time and length, and steppers for the kayak counts. B wins because its numbered sections (When, Your boats, Who's booking) group the fields more clearly, and it visibly collects contact details, which you need to hold a booking. Neither screenshot shows the submit button, a running total or required/optional markers above the fold. A's live '0 of 6 people' counter is a nice touch, but within the cropped view it has no contact section at all. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): The two forms are very similar: both use clear persistent labels, selects for departure time and rental length, and steppers for single and tandem kayaks, all with system fonts and nothing clipped. B pulls slightly ahead because it shows a live '0 of 6 people' counter and lists prices at the top, and a total panel appears to begin at the bottom of its screenshot. A has cleaner numbered groups (When, Your boats, Who's booking). Neither screenshot shows the submit button or required/optional markers, so those scores are uncertain.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both forms use visible labels and constrained controls: steppers for kayak counts and selects for time and duration. A has clearer section headings ('When', 'Kayaks', 'Your details') and better spacing between groups. B shows a running price total right after the trip details, before contact info, whereas no total or submit button is visible in A's screenshot. Neither screenshot shows the submit button or any required/optional markers, so I scored those items on what was visible. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both screenshots stop at about 800px, so neither submit button nor any required/optional marking can be seen, and those scores are low for both. Both use persistent labels, steppers for kayak counts, and selects for time and duration. A shows a running price total before the contact fields. B groups the form more clearly under When, Kayaks and Your details headings, but no price shows in its visible area, so the strengths cancel out.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both forms keep their labels visible and use constrained controls. A uses selects and boat steppers with a 0-of-6 people cap, and B uses a time select and duration radios. B wins because it says everything is required unless marked, labels the mobile number as optional and promises the price before sending. A groups fields better under headings (trip, boats, details) but shows no required/optional distinction. Neither screenshot shows the submit button or total, so item 5 is scored on limited evidence. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): B groups the form better, with headed sections for Your trip, Boats and Your details. Its kayak steppers show the per-hour price and a running '0 of 6 people' count, so the 6-person limit is enforced. A is the only one that explains required versus optional and marks Mobile as optional, but it has no section headings, and B doesn't show which fields are optional. Both screenshots cut off before the submit button and total, so I scored item 5 at 3 for each answer.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers rank the decline-wipe first, flag the silent disabled button and the premature error, and suggest analytics checks. pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers put the fixes in the same sensible order: the decline wipe first, then the silent grey button, then the early errors. Both give concrete wording for error messages. B is slightly better: it keeps more of what the customer typed after a decline (only the CVV is cleared, where A also clears the card number), it gives a clear blur-validation rule, and its funnel checks tell the PM which cause is driving the drop. Neither answer says to show the actual reason a card was declined. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers rank the fixes the same sensible way: the decline wipe first, then the disabled button, then the early error. Both treat placeholder-only labels as a smaller issue but still recommend visible labels. B's replacement error text, "Enter the 16-digit number on the front of your card", is more useful because it tells people how to fix the problem, and B also covers keyboard and screen-reader users and clearing errors once fixed. samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers prefill the right fields from the given context and leave the employee blank for a good reason. A does better on telling managers where a suggestion came from, with hints like 'Usual for Downtown'. B's date default could land on a past day, since the next day after the last shift created may already be over, and its extra 'smart behaviors' section goes a little beyond what was asked. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers prefill the same core fields, leave Employee blank for a good reason, and avoid past dates. B does better on transparency: it shows the source of each suggestion ("Usual for Downtown") and requires real editable values rather than placeholder text. B also adds practical safeguards: use the most common recent value rather than the latest, re-derive when the location changes, and leave fields blank when there is too little history. A's extra sections (chips, sticky values) are useful but stray slightly from the question.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers prefill the same core fields from the given context and correctly keep the employee field blank with good reasons. B is better on the rubric's editability point: it says plainly that prefilled values stay visible and change in one tap, and it adds useful safeguards such as not overwriting manual edits, skipping prefill when there is little data, and ordering fields so choices cascade. Neither answer shows where a suggestion came from, and both date fallbacks (A: the last created shift's date; B: the day after it) could land in the past. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers prefill location, date, times, role and break from sources the request supports, and both leave the employee blank for a well-argued reason. B's same-styling advice hides that source; its date fallback can still land in the past, but it guards the picker against past dates, which A's 'day after last shift' fallback does not, so the trade-offs balance out.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers prefill location, date, times and role sensibly, and both leave the employee blank with a clear reason. B covers neither point, and it leans on employee availability data the tool isn't said to have. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers prefill location, date, times and role from the stated context, and both leave the employee field blank for clear reasons. B is better on item 3: it adds a source hint ('Times from your last shift at Downtown') and one-keystroke overwrite, while A only says values should be visible and cheap to change. samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers reject the two extreme positions, give specific behavior for each field, and say an error should clear live once it's fixed. Answer A recommends checking each field when the person leaves it, which matches the rubric. Answer B defaults to validating on submit and doesn't explain the pile of errors that piles up at the end, though it adds useful accessibility and submit-button advice. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): B recommends checking the email when the person leaves the field and holding back password errors until they leave it or submit, which matches the core rubric point. A defaults to checking only on submit and never mentions leaving the field. Both handle live re-checking, the username pause and the password hint well, but A's case against submit-only is about stale errors rather than a pile of problems at the end.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): B explains why both extremes fail. It recommends checking a field when the person leaves it, using 'touched' state, and adds stale-response handling for the username check. A makes submit the default instead of checking on leaving a field, and it doesn't explain why submit-only validation fails, so it mostly sides with the designer. Both answer the username and password cases well and give concrete behavior for each field. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Answer A recommends validating when the person leaves a field, using a 'touched' rule so untouched fields show no errors, and re-checking live once an error is showing. It also explains the problems with both extremes, including the drawbacks of waiting until submit. Answer B is strong on field details and adds useful extras like input attributes and keeping the button pressable, but it defaults to submit-time validation for email. That means it misses blur-based checking and does not really deal with errors piling up at submit.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Answer A covers both failure modes: errors that appear mid-typing, and a pile of problems that only shows up at submit. It recommends checking on blur and re-checking live once a field has shown an error, and it gives each field its own behavior. Answer B gives excellent per-field detail and useful extras, such as keeping the submit button enabled and showing an error summary. But it leans toward checking only on submit and never recommends checking when the person leaves a field. It also doesn't really name the end-of-form pile-up as a problem. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): B rejects both extremes for the reasons the rubric names: mid-typing errors are false alarms, and checking only at submit leaves a pile of problems at the end. It recommends checking a field when the person leaves it, then re-checking live once an error shows, with sensible handling of the username and password. A says the designer is closer and checks the email only on submit. It also treats checking when someone tabs away as a downside, so it misses the leave-the-field approach, although its per-field table is very concrete.
